routes.description: Establish a historically grounded account of Jesus as the bearer of God's nonviolent kingdom, distinguish theological interpretation from recoverable event claims, and explain divine identity and resurrection as reality-forming metaphor expressed through communal participation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the sources warrant Jesus's kingdom-centered and nonviolent mission while leaving literal divine preexistence and bodily rising historically unverified, and if metaphorical resurrection coherently accounts for vindication, transformed life, and collective hope.

motionBridge.description: Connect the historically recoverable Jesus and the limits of the sources to a coherent metaphorical account of divine identity and resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Show that Gospel redaction, dependence, and theological variation limit confident recovery of eyewitness testimony and literal event claims.
Ground Jesus's identity in his enacted proclamation of God's present kingdom, justice, and nonviolence rather than literal personal preexistence.
Explain resurrection as God's vindication of Jesus and a collective, participatory transformation that is not exhausted by bodily mechanics.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish historical investigation of miracle traditions and their significance from automatic acceptance of supernatural causation.
Establish that metaphor can express consequential reality and sustain allegiance, communal practice, and resistance to imperial violence.

routes.description: Establish a disciplined method for recovering facts about Jesus, defend the early and eyewitness-rooted value of the sources, and use their convergent claims about Jesus's authority, divine identity, empty tomb, appearances, and transformed body to support bodily resurrection.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if ordinary historical criteria yield reliable access to Jesus and early Christian testimony, that testimony supports extraordinary divine identity and a physical resurrection, and historical verification of the event does not require identifying its supernatural cause.

motionBridge.description: Connect historically recoverable early testimony about Jesus's identity and postmortem fate to the conclusion that he underwent bodily resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Show that source proximity, independent attestation, embarrassment, and related criteria can establish facts despite historians' differing interpretive horizons.
Show that early sayings, Pauline material, and Gospel portrayals attribute uniquely divine authority, action, or status to Jesus.
Show that early independent sources describe an empty tomb, appearances, and bodily transformation rather than only changed conduct or symbolic vindication.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish historical verification of an extraordinary event from historical identification of the event's supernatural cause.
Support access to Jesus through distributed early teaching traditions and testimony plausibly rooted in eyewitnesses.

sections.title: Historical Method and Access to Jesus
sections.rationale: The debate depends on what historical inquiry can recover despite interpretive horizons and on whether ordinary authenticity criteria provide warranted access to facts and teachings about Jesus.

sections.title: Gospel Witness, Redaction, and Independence
sections.rationale: Claims about eyewitness roots, evangelists' theological composition, literary dependence, and independent attestation determine how much evidentiary force the Gospel traditions can bear.

sections.title: Jesus's Kingdom Mission and Divine Identity
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing a kingdom-centered, nonviolent account of Jesus with claims that early sources portray him as preexistent, divinely authoritative, and the eschatological judge.

sections.title: Miracles and Extraordinary-Event Inference
sections.rationale: The parties dispute how historians should interpret healings and raisings, whether reported extraordinary events remain historically investigable, and whether event verification can be separated from causal explanation.

sections.title: Bodily and Metaphorical Resurrection
sections.rationale: The principal clash concerns whether the earliest resurrection traditions warrant a physical transformation of Jesus or a collective, participatory metaphor of vindication and transformed life.

routes.description: Move from an assumed fundamental reality through the explanatory demand raised by arbitrary limits to a foundation whose power, positive value, and persistence are maximal, or as great as eliminating arbitrariness permits.
routes.successCriteria: Establish a defensible principle favoring explanations of apparently arbitrary limits, show that unexplained or strongly grounded nonmaximal limits cannot remain at the foundation, secure some foundational greatness, and connect the resulting limit-free attributes to God-like perfection.

motionBridge.description: Show that removing arbitrary limits from fundamental reality warrants maximal or minimally arbitrary power, positivity, and persistence sufficient for God-like perfection.

centralBridges.description: Justify treating an unexplained nonmaximal parameter among apparently equivalent alternatives as an explanatory cost calling for a deeper account.
Establish that fundamental reality possesses some greatness or value from which the removal of arbitrary limitation can proceed.
Show that a strong necessitating ground of an arbitrary limit inherits the relevant arbitrariness, preventing imperfection from being hidden in a deeper foundational property.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how the limits principle can retain defeasible, worldview-relative evidential force within holistic theory comparison.
Distinguish strongly necessitating grounding from indeterministic creation and reconcile the route with fixed divine structure or foundational simplicity.

routes.description: Prevent the limits argument from independently reaching God-like perfection by contesting its explanatory defaults, its attribution of greatness to fundamental reality, and its inference from explained limits to maximal attributes.
routes.successCriteria: Show that holistic non-theistic theories may rationally retain fundamental limits, that rival principles create unresolved symmetry, or that the route lacks an independently warranted bridge from a neutral foundation to mentality, value, and perfection.

motionBridge.description: Show that the limits argument leaves God-like perfection underdetermined because its essential explanatory, axiological, or maximality premises require disputed independent support.

centralBridges.description: Establish that explanatory experience yields only a defeasible default whose exceptions may be warranted by a theory's independent simplicity and explanatory success.
Demonstrate that similarly motivated rival causal principles can oppose traditional theism unless a principled symmetry breaker is supplied.
Show that a mindless foundation may be axiologically neutral and that grounding or enabling derivative value need not confer value on its ground.
Preserve the possibility that an essential, necessary, or deeply explained limitation is non-arbitrary while remaining genuinely nonmaximal.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether arbitrariness inheritance can explain grounded limits without also transmitting created limits to their divine explanation.
Require proposed explanations of fixed divine structure to remain compatible with the accompanying account of divine simplicity and fundamentality.

sections.title: Explanatory Status of Arbitrary Limits
sections.rationale: Covers the definition of arbitrariness and the competing accounts of whether explanatory experience and apparently irrelevant alternatives warrant seeking explanations of fundamental limits.

sections.title: Holistic Theory Comparison and Principle Symmetry
sections.rationale: Addresses the argument's defeasible or worldview-relative force, the role of independent theoretical virtues, and the burden of distinguishing the limits principle from rival principles.

sections.title: Foundational Greatness and Value Grounding
sections.rationale: Tests the indispensable move from a potentially mindless or neutral foundation to some positive value through mentality, grounding, productive capacity, or other greatness-conferring features.

sections.title: Explained Limits and Arbitrariness Inheritance
sections.rationale: Examines whether necessary, essential, or strongly grounded nonmaximal limits remain arbitrary and whether arbitrariness can be inherited without overextending to creative explanation.

sections.title: God-Like Perfection and Divine Models
sections.rationale: Covers the completion of the motion-level inference to maximal power, positivity, and persistence together with challenges arising from fixed divine structure, simplicity, and modal extensions.

routes.description: Establish that scientific explanation and divine agency are compatible, and that a personal creator provides an integrated explanation of rational intelligibility, apparent design, fine-tuning, moral significance, meaning, and the possibility of Christian revelation and miracles.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if theism remains compatible with scientific mechanisms, supplies warranted explanatory advantages over impersonal naturalism, and provides a coherent evidential bridge from a creator to the specifically Christian claims of incarnation, resurrection, redemption, and ultimate justice.

motionBridge.description: Show that science has not displaced God and that Christian theism can still explain the principal phenomena identified by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Explain why rational minds, intelligibility, consciousness, and personhood are grounded more adequately in a personal ultimate reality than in mindless processes.
Connect biological information, cosmic order, and fine-tuning to purposive agency while distinguishing that inference from an appeal to temporary scientific ignorance.
Distinguish regular natural mechanisms from creator agency so that divine action and miracle claims are conceptually compatible with scientific inquiry.
Provide a warranted transition from generic creator theism to Christian revelation, resurrection, forgiveness, moral accountability, and ultimate justice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for objective meaning, enduring hope, and human relational significance without treating their desirability alone as evidence of truth.
Clarify how explanations by mechanism and explanations by agency can coexist without assigning the same explanatory task to each.

routes.description: Establish that natural mechanisms and selection effects explain or undercut the cited evidence for God, that positing a conscious creator compounds rather than resolves the explanatory burden, and that meaning and morality do not require Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal theistic inferences from rationality, design, fine-tuning, miracles, morality, and meaning lack sufficient warrant, while naturalistic accounts remain coherent and the specifically Christian claims require evidence not supplied by their explanatory or emotional appeal.

motionBridge.description: Show that the phenomena in the motion neither require God nor provide adequate grounds for accepting specifically Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Explain apparent biological design and truth-tracking cognition through natural selection without introducing a designing intelligence.
Show why a conscious creator carries an explanatory burden at least as demanding as the natural phenomena the creator is invoked to explain.
Use observer selection and naturalistic alternatives to challenge inferences from intelligibility and fine-tuning while separating unanswered questions from evidence for God.
Require independent evidence for miracles, incarnation, resurrection, and a morally attentive Christian God beyond generic cosmic order or the desirability of religious hope.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Supply non-theistic bases for personal purpose and moral consideration, including evolved cognition, chosen projects, and concern for suffering.
Maintain the distinction between whether a belief offers comfort, hope, or justice and whether the belief is evidentially warranted.

sections.title: Rationality, Minds, and Cosmic Intelligibility
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether rational persons and a lawlike, intelligible universe require grounding in a prior mind or can be accounted for through evolution and observer-selection conditions.

sections.title: Design, Origins, and Fine-Tuning
sections.rationale: This section contains the principal clash over biological information, apparent design, cosmic beginnings, fine-tuning, creator complexity, anthropic alternatives, and the evidential use of unresolved scientific questions.

sections.title: Scientific Explanation, Divine Agency, and Miracles
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether mechanistic science excludes divine agency and whether alleged special divine acts are coherent exceptions within a regular creation or unsupported violations of scientific expectations.

sections.title: Christian Revelation, Resurrection, and Redemption
sections.rationale: The motion concerns Christian theism rather than an unspecified creator, making the bridge from cosmic intelligence to incarnation, resurrection, forgiveness, judgment, and the character of God independently load-bearing.

sections.title: Meaning, Morality, Hope, and Justice
sections.rationale: This section compares theistic and naturalistic accounts of purpose, moral consideration, human value, hope, and ultimate justice while preserving the distinction between existential desirability and evidential truth.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative abductive case in which digital physics, consciousness-related evidence, and introspective idealism make a necessary immaterial mind the most plausible and parsimonious foundation of contingent minds and physical reality.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the three evidential lines support a mind-first ontology, warrant inference beyond directly observed material minds, and identify a necessary mind as a better current explanation than material, simulation-regress, or other non-theistic alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative digital-physics, cosmic-consciousness, and idealist case to good reasons for believing in a necessary immaterial mind.

centralBridges.description: Show that emergent spacetime and mind-like quantum information favor a necessary mind over an unexplained physical base or infinite simulation regress.
Show that consciousness-related evidence and the alleged irreducibility of mind favor consciousness as fundamental rather than wholly produced by matter.
Establish that experienced physical properties can be reduced to mind or information while mental properties resist reduction to material substance.
Justify provisional belief by comparing explanatory scope, probability, parsimony, and revisability across the available hypotheses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why converging indirect evidence can warrant an immaterial mind without direct observation of a brainless mind.
Clarify how the inferred foundational mind can possess the necessity, personality, transcendence, and agency relevant to the theistic conclusion.

routes.description: Show that the affirmative arguments do not meet demonstrability, probability, and burden-of-proof standards because unresolved physical or conscious phenomena do not privilege a necessary immaterial mind over unknown or non-theistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative evidence neither independently demonstrates the proposed mind nor makes it sufficiently probable, and if labeling an under-specified foundation as mind or God adds properties not established by the evidence.

motionBridge.description: Show that the presented arguments fail to provide good reasons for belief in a necessary immaterial mind.

centralBridges.description: Require independently detectable and investigable manifestations connecting the proposed immaterial mind to the phenomena it is offered to explain.
Distinguish being the leading candidate in a limited comparison from being probable enough to warrant belief.
Maintain that exposing defects or unresolved questions in the affirmative case does not require the skeptic to produce a superior complete explanation.
Show that incomplete material accounts, disputed quantum interpretations, and unknown alternatives underdetermine an inference to an immaterial mind.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether inference to a mind without material processing is supported when every observed mind is associated with material processes.
Determine whether calling the proposed foundation mind or God imports agency, personality, timelessness, or religious properties not independently established.

sections.title: Digital Physics, Quantum Measurement, and Observer Dependence
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether emergent spacetime, quantum information, contextuality, and measurement support a mind-first foundation or remain compatible with disputed and incomplete non-conscious physical accounts.

sections.title: Consciousness, Brain Dependence, and Top-Down Causation
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether empirical claims about brains, altered experience, plants, and mental causation undermine material production of consciousness or remain consistent with materially realized minds.

sections.title: Introspective Idealism and Observer-Independent Physical Reality
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether experienced properties and mental information exhaust physical objects or whether unexperienced interactions establish a reality not reducible to consciousness.

sections.title: Abduction, Demonstrability, Probability, and Burden of Proof
sections.rationale: The governing methodological clash is whether present comparative explanatory advantage warrants provisional belief or whether demonstrability, positive probability, and the affirmative burden require substantially more.

sections.title: From an Unknown Foundation to a Necessary Mind or God
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the evidence identifies an immaterial personal mind with relevant divine attributes or merely assigns a theistic label to an under-specified cosmic explanation.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative historical route from early Pauline bodily-resurrection testimony through transmitted Gospel and external witness evidence to an identifiable, structured apostolic community continuous with Catholic Christianity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the early sources warrant bodily rather than merely visionary resurrection belief, the transmission and external evidence remain historically usable, and institutional and doctrinal continuities identify a durable apostolic church despite later disputes.

motionBridge.description: Connect convergent resurrection evidence and early ecclesial continuity into a historically credible account of bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity.

centralBridges.description: Show that the earliest Pauline material describes a transformed bodily resurrection and appearances rather than an exclusively internal vision.
Show that Pauline, Gospel, patristic, and hostile-source lines can be historically combined without depending on a single late tradition.
Trace recognizable offices and a substantially stable doctrinal core through early disputes into the ancient apostolic churches.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use shared councils, fathers, and core doctrines across Roman, Eastern, and Syriac churches as support for a common inheritance.
Distinguish continuity-preserving reform and schism from later developments alleged to constitute substantive doctrinal departure.

routes.description: Establish that the cited sources underdetermine bodily resurrection, that transmission and preservation processes weaken claims of independent corroboration, and that early Christian plurality prevents a secure inference to specifically Catholic continuity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if visionary and inherited-report explanations remain viable, surviving texts and hostile witnesses cannot securely resolve transmission and selection uncertainty, and diverse early communities defeat a determinate linear path to later Catholic identity.

motionBridge.description: Show that the combined evidence does not sufficiently distinguish bodily resurrection and Catholic continuity from viable skeptical historical alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Show that Paul's experience and reports about other witnesses do not independently establish encounters with a resurrected body.
Show that compositional delay, unidentified sources, copying uncertainty, and selective preservation limit the evidential force of surviving materials.
Show that competing communities and retrospective definitions of orthodoxy obstruct a simple continuity inference from earliest Christianity to Catholicism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use differing regional churches and changing historical classifications to test claims of uniform institutional and doctrinal development.
Use pre-Reformation reform and the difficulty of individuating Christian traditions to challenge sharp continuity and departure boundaries.

sections.title: Pauline Evidence for Bodily Resurrection and Appearances
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the earliest cited Christian writings establish a tangible transformed body and bodily encounters, or remain compatible with visionary experience and inherited witness reports.

sections.title: Gospel Sources and Textual Transmission
sections.rationale: The historical force of Gospel material depends on whether the interval before composition, source identification, authorial selection, copying, and possible interpolation permit reliable access to early testimony.

sections.title: Hostile Witnesses and Documentary Preservation
sections.rationale: External descriptions can contribute independent corroboration only insofar as their identification of Christians and their survival are not materially distorted by interpolation or selective preservation.

sections.title: Early Orthodoxy, Diversity, and Ecclesial Structure
sections.rationale: The continuity burden turns on whether early offices and doctrinal convergence identify a persistent apostolic church or whether competing groups, regional variation, and later conciliar definitions make that identity retrospective.

sections.title: Apostolic Continuity, Reform, and Later Christian Divisions
sections.rationale: Comparisons among Catholic, Orthodox, Syriac, Protestant, and medieval reform traditions test which shared doctrines and institutions evidence continuity and where legitimate reform, schism, branching, or departure should be located.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity can coherently recognize suffering as genuinely wrong within a broken creation while relating it to human freedom, divine presence, justice, and promised restoration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the framework explains why suffering is real evil without requiring a purpose for every tragedy, preserves divine goodness and power, and connects present brokenness to morally adequate divine action and future healing.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Christian account makes coherent overall sense of suffering alongside an all-powerful and all-loving God.

centralBridges.description: Explain how a good creation can be presently broken and why its natural mechanisms can produce suffering without making suffering morally illusory.
Account for divine love through God's presence with sufferers, participation in suffering, and action against evil rather than through a distinct benefit assigned to every tragedy.
Show how resurrection, judgment, forgiveness, and future restoration can heal suffering and put wrongs right without disregarding victims or consequences.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground the judgment that suffering and exploitation are objectively wrong rather than merely evolutionarily disfavored.
Explain the roles of consequential human freedom and incomplete present healing within the wider broken-world framework.

routes.description: Establish that suffering is expected under naturalism but creates unresolved tensions among divine omnipotence, perfect love, selective intervention, judgment, and the claimed final defeat of evil.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if apparently gratuitous suffering and the Christian framework's treatment of healing and salvation remain less compatible with an all-powerful, all-loving God than with naturalistic expectations.

motionBridge.description: Show that the observed reality and distribution of suffering make belief in the specified Christian God unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish why an omnipotent and perfectly loving God would need a morally sufficient account of every evil that God knowingly permits.
Show that natural processes can explain suffering and human aversion to it without invoking divine purposes or transcendent moral explanation.
Test whether selective and ambiguous recoveries provide evidence of divine intervention rather than outcomes expected from natural uncertainty.
Determine whether judgment based on belief or reconciliation treats sincere unbelief and grave wrongdoing consistently with perfect love and proportionate justice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Examine whether changing Christian moral practice weakens the claimed explanatory advantage of an objective divine standard.
Assess whether promised resurrection and future healing are sufficiently warranted to resolve rather than postpone the evidential problem.

sections.title: Suffering, naturalism, and the coherence of a broken creation
sections.rationale: This section contains the motion's foundational clash over whether naturalism adequately accommodates suffering or whether Christian broken-creation claims better explain both its mechanisms and its status as a genuine wrong.

sections.title: Evolution, objective morality, and human dignity
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of moral aversion, cooperation, objective norms, and equal dignity bear on whether Christianity supplies explanatory resources that naturalism lacks and whether its historical record affects that claim.

sections.title: Divine presence, permitted evil, and future restoration
sections.rationale: The issue tests whether divine solidarity, epistemic limits, resurrection, and eventual healing can reconcile perfect goodness with permitted atrocities, or whether every permitted evil still demands an adequate greater-good justification.

sections.title: Unanswered prayer and evidence of divine healing
sections.rationale: Selective recovery provides a concrete test of the broken-world and partially realized kingdom account against the contention that natural uncertainty predicts the observed pattern better than purposeful divine intervention.

sections.title: Judgment, forgiveness, freedom, and sincere unbelief
sections.rationale: This section examines whether divine judgment, costly forgiveness, human freedom, and an inclusive invitation can secure justice for victims while treating sincere unbelievers and repentant wrongdoers consistently with perfect love.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Naturalism accommodates suffering as part of nature, whereas divine omnipotence and perfect love imply that every apparently evil event must contribute to a greater good.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly turns to Stephen, and the sustained first-person atheist answer occupies the window until the moderator resumes.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the initial naturalistic contrast and the claimed greater-good tension without answering an earlier locked move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed responsivenessWithinClass values (86 and 91); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is recoverable, but the universal claim that every evil must yield a greater good lacks an explicit doctrinal or logical qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts a necessary greater-good implication, although omnipotence and love alone do not establish that exact formulation without further premises.

charity.alternative: A loving God may oppose evil while permitting some evil for freedom, stable natural order, or reasons not reducible to a benefit from each event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not show that perfect love logically requires a distinct greater good produced by every individual evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (69 and 68); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (62 and 64); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by arguing that suffering creates a foundational inconsistency for the specified God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed representationalCharity values (61 and 62); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says naturalism has no theological evil-explanation problem and expressly claims that Christianity must understand evil as serving a greater good.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: The Christian account of a good but broken creation explains both suffering's natural mechanisms and humanity's conviction that suffering is genuinely wrong.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Sharon directly, and the ensuing extended answer uses her scientific background before the moderator addresses Stephen.

components.text: Whether Christianity can make coherent sense of suffering as real wrongness rather than a theological anomaly.
Whether every evil must be shown to contribute to a particular greater good.

response.rationale: The move contacts the broad coherence challenge by presenting beautiful-but-broken creation and genuine wrongness, but it does not answer the opponent's universal permission inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts the foundational coherence component while leaving the decisive every-evil inference unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is clear, though the causal content of a world being 'broken' remains only partly specified in the selected evidence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The framework plausibly accommodates wrongness, but saying it explains the mechanisms and moral status compresses important warrants.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed logicalCoherence values (77 and 76); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supports the stated framework and phenomenological wrongness, but largely asserts rather than defends the broken-creation explanation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the indispensable broken-creation bridge by explaining how natural mechanisms and genuine moral wrongness coexist.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move develops its own Christian account without materially characterizing or testing a rival interpretation of the opposing argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says the Christian framework validates suffering's wrongness and describes the world as simultaneously beautiful and broken.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evolutionary selection explains widespread aversion to suffering and the social impulse to improve conditions through dispositions favoring survival, reproduction, longevity, and prosperity.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen begins after Sharon asks for naturalistic grounds, answers in a sustained first-person explanation, and yields when Sharon responds.

components.text: Whether Christianity is needed to explain humanity's conviction that suffering is genuinely wrong
Whether natural mechanisms can account for widespread aversion to suffering

response.rationale: The evolutionary account directly supplies a rival natural mechanism for aversion, though it does not establish objective moral wrongness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the natural-mechanism component decisively but only partially answers the distinct objective-wrongness component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evolutionary explanation is recoverable and stable, with the ordinary implicit qualification that selection explains dispositions rather than every judgment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claimed evolutionary pathway fits the limited explanatory aim, although its population-level and dispositional scope is left implicit.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Natural selection coherently explains inherited aversive and social dispositions, with only a bounded implicit bridge from fitness effects to current intuitions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (74 and 76); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central naturalistic-explanation bridge by supplying a non-theistic account of aversion to suffering.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move offers an independent causal explanation and does not rely on a substantive portrayal of the strongest Christian alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes natural selection, inherited social dispositions, and widespread avoidance of suffering among humans and nonhuman animals.

moves.speaker: Sharon Dirckx
moves.proposition: Evolution may explain how moral dispositions arise, but it cannot determine why compassionate norms are objectively better than exploitative survival strategies.
moves.attributionBasis: Sharon takes the floor in direct acknowledgment of Stephen's evolutionary account and develops the counterargument until Stephen announces his rejoinder.

components.text: Whether evolutionary origins can establish that compassionate dispositions are normatively better than exploitative alternatives

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes causal origins from normative authority and argues that selection alone cannot rank competing survival strategies.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts and challenges the decisive inference from evolutionary explanation to moral justification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between causal origins and objective normative ranking is explicit, stable, and scoped to what evolution alone can determine.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that a selection mechanism alone does not normatively rank possible strategies matches the conceptual warrant offered.

charity.alternative: Evolutionary naturalists may combine evolved dispositions with independent moral reasoning rather than derive all normativity from selection itself.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move's criticism succeeds only against the claim that evolutionary mechanism by itself supplies objective ranking.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The is-to-ought distinction is clearly applied, though the further suggestion that the external standard points toward God remains a bounded unsupported bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (79 and 82); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary moral-grounding bridge by challenging selection as a complete source of objective moral ranking.

representationalCharity.rationale: The wording focuses on the mechanism itself and therefore substantially preserves, though does not develop, the strongest naturalistic alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that different moral apparatuses could aid survival and that the evolutionary mechanism itself cannot say which is better.

moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Cooperation can be evolutionarily advantageous, while changing Christian treatment of women and slavery weakens the claim that Christianity uniquely supplies unchanging objective moral guidance.
moves.attributionBasis: Stephen explicitly introduces his rejoinder, develops both evolutionary and historical objections, and stops as Sharon begins her answer.

routes.description: Establish Jesus's death, the empty tomb, and sincere postmortem appearance claims, then argue that bodily resurrection provides the best cumulative explanation of those historical facts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal facts are historically warranted, their earliest interpretation is bodily, and resurrection explains them more adequately than rescue, survival, visionary, or developmental alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative best-explanation inference to the conclusion that Jesus physically rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Roman crucifixion resulted in Jesus's physical death.
Establish that Jesus was buried and that his body was subsequently absent from the tomb.
Establish sincere postmortem appearance claims involving disciples, Paul, and James.
Show that bodily resurrection explains the combined facts better than the competing accounts presented.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that early creedal and Pauline resurrection language referred to bodily raising rather than only spiritual vindication.
Account for apparent source differences without treating the physical resurrection tradition as a later invention.

routes.description: Contest the death, empty-tomb, and physical-appearance premises while showing that early belief and later narrative development permit survival, rescue, visionary, spiritual-vindication, or underdetermined accounts.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a necessary premise remains historically uncertain or if the evidence does not discriminate sufficiently between bodily resurrection and the available nonresurrection interpretations.

motionBridge.description: Connect uncertainty in the premises or inference to the conclusion that physical resurrection is not historically established.

centralBridges.description: Show that the sources do not establish irreversible physical death on the cross with the certainty required by the resurrection inference.
Show that early resurrection and appearance claims need not describe encounters with Jesus's physically revived body.
Show that increasingly explicit physical details can be explained by narrative or theological development.
Demonstrate that rescue, survival, visionary experience, spiritual vindication, or uncertainty remain coherent alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require the affirmative inference to establish its exceptional conclusion without assuming the theological vindication it seeks to prove.
Distinguish early Pauline and creedal material from later tomb and appearance narratives when assessing bodily content.

sections.title: Historical Burden and Best-Explanation Method
sections.rationale: Defines what the affirmative must establish, how cumulative explanatory comparison operates, and whether uncertainty or a coherent alternative is sufficient to defeat the motion.

sections.title: Death by Crucifixion
sections.rationale: Addresses the necessary premise that Jesus irreversibly died, including Roman practice, the duration and details of crucifixion, Pilate's conduct, and proposed survival or rescue interpretations.

sections.title: Burial and the Empty Tomb
sections.rationale: Tests whether bodily absence from a known burial place is historically established and whether early resurrection belief required the original body to leave a tomb.

sections.title: Appearances and Bodily Physicality
sections.rationale: Examines what the disciples, Paul, and James reportedly experienced and whether sincere appearance claims establish encounters with a physically resurrected Jesus rather than visions or spiritual vindication.

sections.title: Early Tradition and Narrative Development
sections.rationale: Evaluates the dating and bodily meaning of creedal and Pauline material, source relationships, Gospel differences, and the claim that explicit physical details intensified over time.

routes.description: Establish a cumulative route from features of the universe, objective morality, the historical case for resurrection, and religious experience to a personal God, then connect that conclusion to Christian theism while answering objections from suffering and religion's record.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its independent considerations jointly make a personal God more plausible than atheistic naturalism, the resurrection consideration supplies the specifically Christian bridge, and the principal defeaters do not overturn that cumulative inference.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative explanatory case and specifically Christian evidence make Christian theism more plausible than atheism across the motion's principal issues.

centralBridges.description: Establish that cosmic origin and life-permitting conditions are better explained by a transcendent personal cause and intelligent design than by necessity, chance, or unaided naturalism.
Establish that objective moral values and duties require a transcendent foundation that theism supplies and atheistic accounts do not.
Establish that the relevant historical facts are best explained by Jesus's resurrection and that this inference connects generic theism to Christian theism.
Show that suffering, evolutionary waste, religious plurality, and harmful religious conduct do not defeat the truth or comparative plausibility of Christian theism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how public arguments may be supplemented by immediate religious experience without making the public cumulative case depend solely on private assurance.
Account for objective meaning, providential justice, and redemption within Christian theism, including for suffering people and those outside explicit Christian history.

routes.description: Withhold the divine hypothesis unless it receives adequate evidential support, challenge the inferences from cosmic and moral phenomena to God, resist the further bridge to Christianity, and present suffering, religious plurality, and religion's authoritative record as contrary considerations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative considerations neither require a divine explanation nor establish the caring and specifically Christian God at issue, while the counterevidence and secular alternatives leave atheistic rejection of that hypothesis warranted.

motionBridge.description: Show that the available considerations do not warrant the divine hypothesis or the further conclusion that a caring, revelatory, specifically Christian God exists.

centralBridges.description: Defend rejection of an unsupported supernatural proposition without assuming an obligation to prove the nonexistence of every proposed deity.
Show that cosmological uncertainty, evolutionary contingency, and secular accounts of morality prevent the relevant phenomena from requiring design or divine moral grounding.
Show that a possible cosmic cause would not establish providence or Christianity and that miracle testimony does not adequately authenticate resurrection, revelation, or doctrine.
Show that severe suffering, cosmic and evolutionary waste, delayed and unequal revelation, and conflicting religions count against benevolent Christian providence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why claims of divine authority demand strong evidence and why scriptural commands and theocratic coercion bear on accepting those claims.
Establish that human solidarity, freedom, ethical life, and meaningful projects remain available without supernatural authority or immortality.

sections.title: Burden of Proof and Religious Epistemology
sections.rationale: The parties' competing accounts of atheism, evidential obligation, cumulative probability, falsifiability, and spiritual assurance determine what must be established before any substantive consideration can support or displace the divine hypothesis.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Fine-Tuning, and Design
sections.rationale: Cosmological origin and fine-tuning form a principal route from observable features of the universe to a personal creator, while uncertainty, evolutionary contingency, waste, and cosmic decay test whether that explanatory inference is warranted.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Its Foundation
sections.rationale: The moral issue tests whether objective values and duties require God, whether evolutionary and social accounts address grounding or only moral development, and whether religious authority contributes anything necessary to ethical life.

sections.title: Resurrection, Miracles, and the Christian Bridge
sections.rationale: The resurrection claim supplies the principal bridge from generic creator theism to Christianity, making the historical facts, miracle testimony, doctrinal authentication, and the scope and timing of revelation structurally indispensable.

sections.title: Suffering, Evil, and Benevolent Providence
sections.rationale: Suffering and apparent waste directly test the compatibility and comparative plausibility of an omnipotent, knowledgeable, and good God, including whether sufficient reasons, redemption, and eternal compensation answer the objection.

sections.title: Religion's Record, Authority, and Human Meaning
sections.rationale: Religion's commands and institutional consequences bear on claims of revelation and authority, while the competing accounts of objective purpose, secular solidarity, liberty, and mortality address the motion's broader contrast between Christian theism and atheism.

routes.description: Establish that human sin must be reconciled consistently with God's holiness and justice, and that the biblical witness identifies Christ's voluntary atonement and righteousness as God's sufficient means of reconciliation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects humanity's sinful condition to the need for a just ground of forgiveness, establishes Christ's identity and sacrificial work from scripture, and explains good deeds as consequences rather than the basis of acceptance.

motionBridge.description: Show that grace through Christ's atonement supplies a coherent and biblically grounded account of forgiveness, reconciliation, and moral transformation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that humanity's relation to sin and God's holy moral standard creates a need that direct moral effort cannot resolve.
Explain why divine forgiveness requires a non-arbitrary ground that preserves the relation between God's justice, holiness, and law.
Ground Christ's identity, voluntary sacrifice, priestly role, resurrection, and sufficient righteousness in the biblical witness.
Distinguish the ground of salvation in Christ from the resulting role of transformed conduct and obedience.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend continuity among the Old Testament sacrificial and prophetic materials and the New Testament account of Christ.
Provide a consistent basis for treating the relevant biblical writings and their textual transmission as authoritative evidence.

routes.description: Establish that accountable deeds, sincere repentance, restitution, and God's direct mercy form a coherent salvation account, while disputing the moral necessity and uniform scriptural pedigree of Christ's substitutionary atonement.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it shows that people remain morally capable and accountable, that direct forgiveness can be just and principled, and that the Quran and relevant biblical materials support this model more consistently than atonement theology.

motionBridge.description: Show that direct divine forgiveness joined to repentance and moral accounting is coherent and grounded in the Quran and relevant biblical teachings.

centralBridges.description: Establish that people can perform morally significant good, repent, repair harm, and be judged without inherited guilt or absolute incapacity.
Explain how God may forgive directly while maintaining equitable judgment, moral responsibility, and justice.
Challenge the necessity and coherence of transferring punishment or righteousness through Christ's sacrificial death.
Ground direct forgiveness and accountable deeds in the Quran, the Old Testament, and teachings attributed to Jesus while contesting their displacement by later atonement theology.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify why continuing requirements for good conduct bear on the claimed sufficiency and practical role of atonement.
Supply a principled account of the differing authority, provenance, and interpretive treatment assigned to Quranic and biblical materials.

sections.title: Human Sin, Moral Capacity, and Inherited Condition
sections.rationale: The competing accounts depend on whether humanity inherits a disabling sinful condition requiring a representative remedy or remains capable of accountable good, repentance, and restoration under merciful judgment.

sections.title: Divine Holiness, Justice, and Direct Forgiveness
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether pardon requires an objective satisfaction of divine law or whether God can forgive repentant people directly without compromising holiness, fairness, or principled moral judgment.

sections.title: Christ's Identity, Sacrifice, and the Atonement Mechanism
sections.rationale: The motion centrally requires examining whether Christ's identity and voluntary sacrificial role make atonement coherent and sufficient, or whether substitution, transferred punishment, and priestly sacrifice remain conceptually or scripturally unsupported.

sections.title: Grace, Good Deeds, and the Ground of Salvation
sections.rationale: The sides must distinguish whether deeds obtain or preserve salvation, express an already received salvation, or operate within a merciful system of repentance and moral accounting.

sections.title: Scriptural Continuity, Development, and Authority
sections.rationale: Claims about the Old Testament, Paul, the Gospels, Hebrews, and the Quran determine whether either salvation model represents a continuous revealed teaching or depends on disputed development, authorship, transmission, and interpretive standards.

routes.description: Establish that objective evaluative facts are required to account for rational assessment and that moral appearances can provide defeasible justification without first earning support through best-explanation reasoning.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it supports objective moral facts against desire-based and projectivist alternatives, establishes a defensible appearance-based source of prima facie justification, and connects that epistemology to basic moral knowledge.

motionBridge.description: Connect the case for irreducible evaluative facts with a route from moral appearances to justified moral belief and knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Show that rationally assessing desires, actions, and suffering requires truth-valued evaluative standards rather than attitudes alone.
Establish that appearances confer defeasible prima facie justification and are epistemically prior to explanatory inference.
Show that understanding evaluative and experiential subject matter can justify elementary moral judgments as instances of a priori knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how evaluative judgments can shape desires, emotions, and conduct rather than merely projecting antecedent attitudes.
Identify necessary judgments that resist reduction to linguistic or conceptual analyticity and thereby support broader rationalism.

routes.description: Establish that normative reasons depend on an agent's desires and deliberative standpoint, while moral belief lacks justification because objective moral facts are unnecessary in the best explanation of moral experience.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it accounts for reasons and moralized conduct without objective value, defends an explanatory standard for evidence, and shows that moral facts neither ground categorical reasons nor contribute indispensable explanatory work.

motionBridge.description: Connect the denial of attitude-independent value with the claim that moral belief lacks the evidence required for moral knowledge.

centralBridges.description: Ground normative reasons in desires, goals, values, or an agent's deliberative perspective rather than categorical demands.
Require justified belief to arise from causally informed explanatory support and show that moral facts are evidentially idle.
Explain the acquisition of concepts and causal models without presupposing contentful appearances accepted as initially true.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for moral judgment and continued moralized conduct through projected values, emotions, and stable concerns.
Interpret mathematical and modal reflection through conceptual application, experiential relations, or a broadened account of analyticity.

sections.title: Objective Value and the Error-Theoretic Burden
sections.rationale: This issue frames the motion-level dispute over whether elementary moral judgments track attitude-independent facts or whether value is exhausted by human attitudes and practices.

sections.title: Desires, Reasons, and Rational Authority
sections.rationale: The existence of categorical reasons is the principal metaphysical pathway between theories of agency and the existence or nonexistence of objective moral obligations.

sections.title: Appearances, Explanation, and Epistemic Foundations
sections.rationale: This issue directly determines whether moral appearances may justify belief prima facie or whether evidence requires causal and best-explanation support that leaves moral facts idle.

sections.title: Moral Belief, Emotion, and Projection
sections.rationale: The causal relationship among judgment, desire, emotion, and conduct bears on whether moral thought responds to facts or projects antecedent evaluative attitudes.

sections.title: A Priori Knowledge, Concepts, and Analyticity
sections.rationale: The scope of a priori justification tests whether reflection can disclose substantive truths about suffering and badness or only relations internal to concepts and their application.
